activities.anchor: a blood cell's load in a centrifuge
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the quadratic cruelty of cornering
activities.name: cmCornerCloze

config.text: Double the cornering speed and the required grip multiplies by %%0%%, because both the momentum to bend and the rate of bending grow. On a wet road (μ ≈ 0.4) the 50 m corner's limit falls to about %%1%% km/h — whatever the sign says.
config.hint: F = mv²/r hides a square; √(0.4 × 9.8 × 50) hides a square root.

activities.anchor: the way the surface or field actually pushes
activities.caption: bet first — what holds the water in the overhead bucket?
activities.name: cmBucketPredict

config.q: A child whirls a bucket of water overhead without spilling a drop. At the top of the swing, what keeps the water pressed in the bucket?
choices: Centrifugal force pushing the water outward against the bucket's base
The bucket's base pushing inward on the water — the only real force there is
The water's stickiness to the bucket outweighing gravity at the top
config.why: There is no outward push to draw on: every real force points the way the surface actually pushes. The bucket's base supplies the inward centripetal force — and the whirl must be quick enough that at the top the required v²/r is at least g.

activities.anchor: and every planet, tide and galaxy since
activities.caption: call the magnitude — how hard does Earth pull the Moon?
activities.name: cmMoonEstimate

config.prompt: The Moon is about 60 Earth-radii away. Roughly how strong is Earth's gravitational grip up there, in m/s²?
config.why: 9.8 / 60² ≈ 0.0027 m/s² — and the Moon's measured centripetal acceleration (v²/r from its 27.3-day period) matches it exactly. The falling Moon IS the falling apple.
config.context: About 0.03% of what you feel standing up — inverse-square is a brutal discount.

activities.anchor: all sit on the same T²/r³ curve
activities.caption: pair each orbit with its period
activities.name: cmPeriodsMatch

config.prompt: One T²/r³ curve covers them all — match each resident of orbit to its period:
config.why: Slide outward and the demanded speed falls as 1/√r while the circle lengthens — the period grows as r^(3/2), Kepler's third law explained by Newton's inverse square.

activities.anchor: the moment physics and astronomy became the same subject
activities.caption: place your own orbital speed on the scale
activities.name: cmSpeedPlace

config.prompt: You are moving around the Sun right now. Place Earth's orbital speed on the scale (km/s):
config.why: Earth orbits at about 30 km/s — sustained by nothing but your own inertia while the Sun's grip curves you around. Mercury runs 47 km/s; Neptune, thirty times farther out, ambles at 5.4.
config.context: The speed ladder is v = √(GM/r) — closer means faster, no exceptions.

activities.anchor: the calcium in your bones is stellar shrapnel
activities.caption: file the stellar endings — how does each star retire?
activities.name: cmStarBuckets

config.prompt: Sort each fate into the right ending:

items.label: the Sun's own retirement, after swelling into a red giant
an Earth-sized ember left behind by puffed-off outer layers
the explosive death of a star that burned hot and fast
leaves a neutron star behind — a sugar-cube outweighing a mountain
the forges where calcium and iron were made
gravity's endgame, past a mass limit

config.why: Low-mass stars retire quietly as white dwarfs; massive ones die young in supernovae — forging the heavy elements and leaving neutron stars — and the most massive collapse past rescue into black holes.

activities.anchor: gravity has been sculpting ever since
activities.caption: slide the divider — the Sun today vs the Sun after the fuel runs out
activities.name: cmSunCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider between the Sun's two acts:

before.label: Now — main sequence
before.text: The core, squeezed to about 15 million kelvin, fuses hydrogen into helium: 4 million tonnes of mass become energy every second, holding the star inflated against its own gravity for roughly 10 billion years.

after.label: Later — red giant, then white dwarf
after.text: The fuel runs out and the balance tips: the Sun swells into a red giant, puffs off its outer layers as a nebula, and retires as a white dwarf — an Earth-sized ember.

config.why: A stellar life is fusion against gravity; when the hydrogen runs out, the same two forces stage the ending.

activities.anchor: the auroras are that traffic visible
activities.caption: file the metals — what does a magnet actually grab?
activities.name: magStickBuckets

config.prompt: The scrapyard crane is waiting. File each metal:

items.label: steel — the car body the crane lifts

config.why: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt (plus a few rare alloys) respond; aluminium, copper, brass and gold are unmoved — which is why the crane lifts the car but not its wiring.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the grip rule and the on-switch magnet
activities.name: magGripCloze

config.text: Right-hand grip rule: your thumb points along the %%0%%, and your fingers curl the way the field goes. Coiled into a solenoid with an iron core, that becomes a magnet with an %%1%% — and MRI scanners run fields some %%2%% times Earth's.
config.hint: Ørsted's compass told you what goes with the thumb; the iron core sets the factor.

activities.caption: rebuild the motor's spin cycle — where the commutator earns its keep
activities.name: magMotorOrder

config.prompt: Put the d.c. motor's rotation loop in order:
items: Current flows through the loop sitting in the magnetic field
Opposite sideways forces on the loop's two sides form a couple
Every half-turn, the split-ring commutator reverses the current through the loop
The torque never changes sign, so the spin keeps going
config.why: The commutator is the clever part: without the half-turn reversal, the couple would flip sign and the loop would oscillate around its resting position instead of spinning.

activities.anchor: the demo of Lenz in real time
activities.caption: bet first — slit the tube and what changes?
activities.name: magTubePredict

config.q: A magnet falls in slow motion down a copper tube. Now cut the tube open lengthwise and drop the magnet through again. What happens?
choices: It still falls slowly — copper's magnetism brakes it all the same
It falls normally — an unbroken loop is what lets the opposing induced currents exist
It falls faster than free fall — with Lenz removed, the field now assists
config.why: Lenz's braking needs circulating induced currents, and a slit tube has no loop for them. No changing-flux circuit, no opposition — and remember copper was never ferromagnetic to begin with.

activities.anchor: a motor's trick run in reverse
activities.caption: pair each machine with its trick
activities.name: magMachinesMatch

config.prompt: One law, many machines — match each to what it actually does:

pairs.right: a split-ring commutator reverses the current every half-turn
a spinning coil makes the flux swing sinusoidally — mains, made literal
the coil's force oscillates a cone at the signal's frequency
the loudspeaker run backwards — motion induces the signal

config.why: Supply current and get motion, or supply motion and get current — F = B·I·L one way, EMF = −N·ΔΦ/Δt the other, same two actors.

activities.anchor: expensive power electronics to play in transformers' territory
activities.caption: place the phone charger's turns ratio on the scale
activities.name: magChargerPlace

config.prompt: A phone charger steps 230 V mains down to 12 V. Place the ratio of primary turns to secondary turns (N₁ per N₂) on the scale:
config.why: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁, so the primary needs about 230/12 ≈ 19 turns for every secondary turn.
config.context: The same lever, run the other way, takes generation at ~25 kV up to 400 kV for transmission.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the free-energy claim
activities.name: magStepSpot

config.prompt: One line of this transformer answer is wrong — click it:
lines: A step-up transformer converts 12 V to 230 V, so V₂/V₁ ≈ 19.2.
Power delivered by the secondary is greater than power drawn by the primary — the transformer amplifies energy.
With 99% efficiency, a 100 W primary draw delivers about 99 W to the secondary.
The secondary current falls in the same proportion the voltage rose: about 8.3 A down to 0.43 A.
That trade is why the grid transmits at 400 kV: tiny current, tiny I²R loss.
config.correction: Power out ≈ power in — voltage is multiplied at the cost of current divided in the same proportion; the transformer is a gear lever, not an energy source.
config.why: The bookkeeping balances: 100 W in, ~99 W out. Step the voltage 19× and the current drops 19× — which is the entire grid trick, not free energy.
